2.text: “Then they came to the place where the race was to be held, and he outran all the drivers

3.text: and took the prize. Afterwards, when fighting he used the bow and the arrow as he did in his

4.text: boyhood. He shot all at once, and killed his adversary.”

5.text: Another hero, Êˊɪrg̣ɪn, is also described as a young archer, light of foot

6.text: and quick at shooting. Near the entrance of a narrow passage between the

7.text: mountains, young Êˊɪrg̣ɪn is standing. He is drinking water from a wooden

8.text: bowl. He sees a Cossack warrior clad in full armor coming to him. “Drink

9.text: your fill,” says the Cossack. “That is your last drink on earth.” The Cos-

10.text: sack brandishes his spear. Êˊɪrg̣ɪn takes his bow, and puts on the string a

11.text: small arrow of whalebone. The face of the Cossack is covered all over with

12.text: iron, only two holes are left for the eyes. He shoots and hits him in the

13.text: right eye through the hole of the visor. The Cossack falls down and is

15.text: Other warriors are also mentioned, but they do not play an important role.

16.text: Those whose names han been given are known in various parts of the Chuk-

17.text: chee territory. I met families who claim descent from one or the other of

18.text: these ancient heroes. “We count nine generations (sometimes eight, rarely

19.text: less than that) from such and such a one,” is the usual expression. “We trace

20.text: our lineage.” And the families with such a lineage claim a certain superiority

21.text: over others, though by the other people these pretensions are but little heeded.

22.text: The Taˊn˙ñɪt of these tales are, as stated before, Reindeer Koryak. They

23.text: are always described as very rich in reindeer, considerably more so than the

24.text: Chukchee. They have certain fortresses (wuiˊwun, pl. wuiˊwut, a term used

25.text: at present for single block-houses, and also villages of the Russians and Rus-

26.text: sianized natives, composed of such block-houses). It is not easy to understand

27.text: what kind of fortresses these wuiˊwut may have been. The details of the

28.text: description are insufficient to form any judgment. For instance: “Then the

29.text: Taˊn˙ñɪt shut themselves up in the wuiˊwun. They broke down another wuiˊ-

30.text: wun, and covered the walls of the first with its wood. On the roof, near

31.text: the vent-hole, is a second story. The best archers stand there and shoot

32.text: downwards on the assailants.” Perhaps it is simply the underground house

33.text: of the Maritime Koryak,¹ with the wooden storm-roof around the vent-hole.

34.text: Such houses are quite suitable for use as strongholds. The Russian accounts

35.text: of the wars with the Koryak, in the first half of the eighteenth century, mention

36.text: quite frequently small fortresses in which the Koryak used to defend them-

37.text: selves, and which were taken by the Russians. The same may be said of

38.text: the Kamchadal. All such fortresses, however, belong to the Maritime people.
